description: We're a Vienna team tackling the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. We're building an open-source web tool that shows mission planners, teachers and the public where and when a lunar south pole landing site gets sunlight for power and line-of-sight to Earth for communication, using real NASA terrain and ephemeris data.
summary: Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an open-source web app that shows where and when a lander at the Moon's south pole gets sunlight for power and a line of sight to Earth for radio. Pick any spot on the Moon – from a list of Apollo, robotic and Artemis III candidate sites or by clicking the map – and any hour from 2026 to 2030. The app instantly shows the Sun's and Earth's elevation above the real local horizon, how long until sunset or Earthset, and a timeline of light and radio. It traces each horizon over NASA LOLA terrain and uses NASA/JPL SPICE ephemerides, so mountains that block the Sun or Earth are taken into account. Two sites can be compared side by side, and the app lists the longest windows with both power and radio. This matters because at the south pole the Sun stays just above the horizon: a few kilometres can decide between continuous power and a mission-ending night. Our tool turns that complex geometry into a clear map anyone can understand.
details:
What it does: The Lunar Landing Site Navigator answers two questions for any point on the Moon: Is there sunlight for solar power, and is Earth above the horizon for direct radio contact? It works for any date and hour from 2026 to 2030.

How it works: A Python pipeline reads NASA's LOLA south-pole elevation model (80 m/px) and traces the true horizon in 360 directions for every point within 170 km of the pole. Sun and Earth positions come from NASA/JPL SPICE (DE421 ephemeris, lunar orientation kernels). The web app re-computes everything live in the browser for any clicked point.

Features: whole-Moon 3D globe with NASA LROC imagery; 3D south-pole terrain with map layers (light and radio now, illumination, Earth visibility, both together, longest night, slope); curated Apollo, robotic and Artemis III sites plus custom coordinates; date/time control with playback; countdown to sunset and Earthset; timeline and 360° sky view; side-by-side comparison of two sites; list of the longest power-and-radio windows; direct link to the same spot in NASA's LROC QuickMap; English and German.

Results: For example, a point on the rim of Shackleton crater has power and radio 43 % of the time in 2027–2028, compared with 24 % at the Haworth candidate region, with a best window of almost 16 days in a row.

Tools: Python, SpiceyPy, NumPy, Numba, rasterio; TypeScript, React, three.js, Vite, Tailwind CSS, uPlot; unit tests check the browser physics against the Python results.

Why it is creative: Instead of static maps, anyone – mission planners, students, the public – can explore light and radio over time in an interactive 3D view and see exactly which mountain blocks the Sun.

Factors we considered: accuracy of terrain and ephemerides, the Earth's motion in the sky through libration, partial visibility of the Sun's disc, fast loading in the browser, and plain-language explanations for non-experts. The whole project is open source under the MIT licence.
